source.title: Understanding the Effects of Safety Unalignment on Reasoning- and Instruction-Tuned Large Language Models

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly adapts the weight-orthogonalization method based on a harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference refusal vector, then evaluates refusal and capability outcomes on additional instruction-tuned and reasoning models.
record.gate_note: The study reports refusal rates after weight orthogonalization and capability evaluations of the edited models. Candidate-vector values used to select the final refusal vector are not outcomes and are not rows. JT comparisons are not rows because JT does not apply or test the refusal direction. SFT results are not included as rows because they evaluate a subsequent mitigation rather than the direction-removal intervention.
record.test_reason: The study reuses the original codebase to compute a harmful-minus-harmless mean-difference vector and orthogonalize the weights against it. It then measures StrongREJECT refusal rates and capability benchmarks on three released instruction-tuned models and three reasoning models. These results bear directly on V1 (ablation plus capability retention), V2 (weight edit on released models) and V8 (reasoning models).
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct, with additions. The authors say WO and JT split refusal degradation (each wins on three models), but WO keeps helpfulness (2.2% average drop vs 13.4% for JT), adds far fewer hallucinations, and yields stronger adversarial and cyber attackers. WO cuts refusal much less in reasoning models (29.3%) than in instruction-tuned ones (74.4%). Benign SFT mitigates much of WO's attack uplift but not its cyber-attack uplift consistently.
record.recipe_differences: The paper directly adapts the original weight-orthogonalization code and computes harmful-minus-harmless candidate vectors across layers and post-instruction positions, selecting a vector by refusal suppression and orthogonalizing weights. It evaluates StrongREJECT refusal rates and helpfulness benchmarks on six models, including reasoning counterparts; it does not test activation addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary by model and training stage: the paper reports smaller refusal reductions for reasoning models than instruction-tuned models overall, and the per-model WO refusal rates differ substantially.

fits_no_version.finding: WO-edited models are more effective attackers on AutoDAN-Turbo and CyberSecEval 3 than both the aligned models and jailbreak-tuned models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-direction removal unlocks downstream harmful capability, not just compliance.

fits_no_version.finding: Subsequent benign SFT on OpenHermes restores 40.5–69.8% of refusal in WO models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Ablated refusal directions can be re-learned through ordinary instruction tuning.

record.problems: The paper reports no uncertainty estimates for the listed outcomes. The reported refusal measure is StrongREJECT refusal rate; the direction is selected using validation instructions and Llama Guard 2. Some reasoning models retain substantial refusal after orthogonalization, and some general-helpfulness task scores decline.
record.rows_left_out: Because the 60-row limit was reached, the WO results for ARC-C, HellaSwag, PIQA, and Winogrande are omitted for all 12 models; these are separately reported in Table 5. JT results are not included because they do not apply the refusal-vector intervention.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal. Activation-level ablation as distinct from the weight edit. Any direction other than the single selected vector.
Community 'abliterated' releases or other abliteration toolchains; only this paper's own edits are tested.
Direction addition. Where in the reasoning trace refusal is decided. Whether the direction differs between the thinking and answer phases.

missing.what: TruthfulQA and TofuEval hallucination rates for WO models. TruthfulQA rises after WO in all six models, e.g. Llama-3.1-8B* 58.7 to 64.9 and Qwen2.5-14B* 54.7 to 60.1.
WO results on ARC-C, HellaSwag, PIQA and Winogrande. Declared in rows_left_out, but needed for the reasoning models, e.g. Qwen3-4B* ARC-C 48.0 to 43.1.

record.verdict_notes: Refusal is judged by the StrongREJECT fine-tuned evaluator, not the original substring or Llama Guard scoring; Llama Guard 2 was used only to select the vector. Reasoning-model baselines are already low (39–45% for the two R1 distills), which limits how much reduction is possible. No uncertainty estimates are given and refusal used greedy decoding. Single author, preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Tests weight orthogonalization and refusal rates, not literal projection of the direction out of every activation position; does not test adding the direction or measure every other ability.
Tests weight orthogonalization on the named models, but does not use the term abliteration or test a separate deployment or release process.
No test of attacks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
No comparison of one direction with an affine, cone, or multiple-direction account.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
Each model has its own refusal vector calculated; no cross-language or cross-model vector transfer is evaluated.
No test of when or how refusal training determines whether one removable direction exists.
Tests weight orthogonalization and refusal rates in reasoning-tuned models, but not activation projection or direction addition.

relation.reason: It reports its own refusal rates and capability scores before and after the weight edit on six released models. These bear directly on V1, V2 and V8.

tranche.reason: The paper directly adapts the Arditi et al. codebase: DIM candidates over post-instruction positions and layers, selection with Llama Guard 2, then weight orthogonalization. It measures refusal rate on harmful prompts plus capability benchmarks. Only the judge differs (StrongREJECT evaluator). The reasoning-model results add a T3-like extension.

source_check.notes: Capability rows R13–R32 are linked to V2, but V2 (weight edit removes refusal) makes no capability claim, so drop that link. R29 is labelled partial, yet the V8 supports verdict cites it as near-baseline; it should be observed. Two checkpoint caveats: the reasoning models are released checkpoints (Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B), not made by the authors; and Table 1 gives 'Qwen2.5-14B' (a base-model name) despite calling it instruction-tuned. On method: the study has no random-direction control (its 'controls' are the aligned baselines and the JT comparison); results come from single greedy runs with no uncertainty; and '% Decr.' values are relative decreases, not percentage points.

statements.correction: 2604.02574 belongs under limits_scope. WO refusal: Qwen3-4B* 81.2->70.6 (13.0% relative decrease), Llama-3.1-8B* 45.4->26.2 (42.3%), Qwen2.5-14B* 39.3->26.5 (32.5%).
